blocks.heading: Where could P&G's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted price is $147.52 in October 2027, a total return of 0% including dividends. It reaches $149.96 in October 2028, equal to a 5% total return. By October 2029, it reaches $156.46, equal to a 12% total return. The bear-to-bull range then spans $103.66 to $214.27. Today's price is $151.23.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for P&G?

paragraphs.text: The base uses management's $7.00 FY2027 core-EPS midpoint and organic-sales guidance of 1%–3%. Management also expects a weak first quarter followed by improvement in the second half. Flat FY2026 organic volume and mixed category share support the bear case, while Beauty's volume growth and upgraded Tide sales support the bull case.

blocks.heading: How much cash does P&G really make?

paragraphs.text: P&G’s adjusted free cash flow adds back payments under the 2017 U.S. Tax Act. That improves comparability because the payments relate to an earlier obligation, but the cash still left the company. Stock compensation deserves a similar check: it costs no immediate cash when shares are issued, but it transfers value to employees and can dilute owners. Deducting FY2026’s $524 million from free cash flow gives a stricter analytical view.

blocks.heading: How much does P&G pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The latest declared quarterly rate annualizes to $4.354. P&G has raised its dividend for 70 consecutive years, and FY2026 free cash flow was $15.147 billion against $10.232 billion of dividends paid. That supports gradual base increases, a pause rather than a cut in the bear case, and larger raises only if cash recovery accelerates.

blocks.heading: Does P&G's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Capital expenditure is money spent on factories, equipment and production capacity. Free cash flow is the operating cash left after that spending. Across the five years shown, P&G reinvested $17,722 million in capital expenditure. It generated $73,068 million of free cash flow and paid shareholders $81,075 million through dividends, buybacks and payments to minority owners. FY2024 was the only year in which those distributions left a surplus.

P&G can pay out more than one year’s free cash flow because it can also use asset-sale proceeds, existing cash, employee share-plan receipts or borrowing. That is not automatically unhealthy, but it leaves less room for acquisitions without another funding source. For the next fiscal year, P&G planned about $10 billion of dividends and $5 billion of repurchases.

blocks.heading: What has P&G guided for FY2027?

paragraphs.text: For FY2027, management guides to 1%–3% organic sales growth and 0%–3% core EPS growth. The core EPS midpoint is $7.00. Adjusted free-cash-flow productivity is expected at 85%–90%. Higher raw materials, energy and transportation costs are expected to create $1,000 million of after-tax pressure.

blocks.heading: Did P&G keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: P&G’s fiscal 2026 promise was organic-sales and core-EPS growth ranging from flat to 4%. Both finished at 1%. That met the stated range, but fell below its midpoint, so the promise was kept in the narrow sense without delivering the central expectation.

blocks.heading: How have P&G revenue and profit trended over the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: Profit weakened more clearly. Gross margin fell from 49.1% to 48.5%, and diluted EPS fell from $1.48 to $1.26. Restructuring caused part of the decline, but core EPS also fell 3%. Productivity savings were offset by marketing, product and packaging investment, unfavorable mix and higher commodity costs.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in P&G's next results?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is the anticipated October 22, 2026 first-quarter earnings call. Investors should watch market share, consumer demand and confidence in the rest of the year, not just whether EPS beats a forecast. P&G reported that fourth-quarter sell-out rose 2% while sell-in fell 1%.
